09-006.r: Justin (Greek writer) called Chandragupta Maurya 'Sandrocottos' and described his meeting with Alexander; William Jones first identified Sandrokottos as Chandragupta Maurya.
09-006.t: Arrian and Plutarch called him 'Androkottus'; don't confuse with Chandragupta I or II (Gupta kings).

09-008.r: Justin, a Greek writer → described the meeting of Sandrokottos (Chandragupta Maurya) with Alexander the Great.
09-008.t: Not Pliny, Strabo or Megasthenes; the 'meeting with Alexander' account is Justin's.

09-009.r: Kautilya (Chanakya, Vishnugupta) → prime minister, advisor and chief priest of Chandragupta Maurya; pioneer of political science, author of Arthashastra.

09-010.r: Chanakya's other (childhood) name → Vishnugupta; the Arthashastra names its author Kautilya, and one verse calls him Vishnugupta.
09-010.h: Three names, one man: Chanakya (son of sage Chanak), Kautilya, Vishnugupta.

09-012.r: Kautilya's Arthashastra → treatise on polity, statecraft and principles of government; also covers administration and agrarian system, so 'more than one' option fits.
09-012.h: Saptanga order: Swami, Amatya, Janapada, Durg, Kosa, Danda, Mitra - King first, Ally last.

09-014.r: Saptanga theory of State → Mitra (Ally) is the seventh part; the Ally is like the ear of the state, helping the king in peace and war.
09-014.t: Janapada (territory), Durga (fort) and Kosha (treasury) are earlier elements, not the seventh.

09-015.r: Kautilya's Arthashastra mainly deals with political policies; a unique saga of political policy and a rich source on the Mauryan dynasty.

09-016.r: Arthashastra (Dasa-Kalpa chapter): judicial punishment could make one a slave; a female slave bearing her master's son became free; that son got no legal status as master's son.

09-017.r: Kautilya's Arthashastra → compared with 'The Prince' of Machiavelli, the Italian political thinker.

09-018.r: Deimachus → ambassador of Syrian king Antiochus I Soter to Bindusara's court (per Strabo); he replaced Megasthenes.
09-018.t: Don't confuse Deimachus (sent to Bindusara) with Megasthenes, whom he replaced.

09-019.r: Samant Pasadika of Buddhaghosa → says Ashoka won Avanti Mahajanapada and merged it into the Mauryan empire during Bindusara's rule.

09-020.r: Chandragupta Maurya's palace at Pataliputra → made of wood (80-pillared, wooden floors); Kumrahar = palace remains, Bulandibagh = city wall; excavated by D.B. Spooner.
09-020.h: Kumrahar = King's hall; Bulandibagh = boundary wall.

09-023.r: Chandragupta Maurya (founder) → conquered the Deccan, shown by Jain and Tamil sources; Ashoka conquered only Kalinga.

09-024.r: Greek texts called Pataliputra (modern Patna) 'Polibrotha' / Palibothra.

09-025.r: Chandragupta Maurya → first king to conquer Malwa, Gujarat and Maharashtra; Junagadh inscription of Rudradaman proves his sway over western India.

09-026.r: Not linked to Chandragupta Maurya → Sanchi (Ashoka's stupa). Linked: Susima (grandson), Vishnugupta (his mentor Kautilya), Junagadh inscription (governor Pushyagupta, Sudarshan lake).

09-027.r: Junagarh Rock Inscription of Rudradaman → proves Chandragupta Maurya ruled western India (Gujarat); records governor Pushyagupta building Sudarshan lake.
09-027.t: Not Ashoka's Girnar or Sopara edicts; the proof comes from a later Shaka king, Rudradaman.

09-029.r: Chandragupta Maurya defeated Seleucus, governor of the eastern Macedonian empire (Sindh-Afghanistan), in 305 BC.

09-031.r: Sudarshana Lake (Girnar, Saurashtra) → built under Chandragupta Maurya by governor Pushyagupta; later repaired by Ashoka, Rudradaman and Skandgupta.
09-031.h: Builder C, repairers A-R-S: Ashoka, Rudradaman, Skandgupta.

09-032.r: Map covering almost all India except Assam and parts of the far south → Ashoka's empire towards the close of his reign.

09-033.r: Ashoka → based his Rajdharma/Dhamma on three bases: longanimity (patience), liberty and compassion; ethical, not tied to any community.

09-034.r: Ashoka's Dhamma drew on Rahulovada-Sutta (also Lakkhana Sutta, Dhammapada); Dhamma-Mahamatras appointed in the 14th year of his reign. Both statements correct.

09-035.r: Sri Lanka (Tamraparni) → not in Ashoka's empire; Rock Edict II names Chola, Pandya, Satiyaputta, Keralaputta and Tamraparni as edge (border) states.

09-036.r: Major Rock Edict II → mentions South Indian kingdoms: Chola, Pandya, Satiyaputta, Keralaputta. Ashoka has 14 major rock edicts.

09-037.r: Ashoka → built India's first hospitals and herbal (medicinal) gardens; also dug wells and planted shade trees.

09-038.r: Ashoka's epithet 'Devanampriya' (beloved of the Gods) → shows he kept faith in Hinduism though Buddhist; coronation 269 BC.

09-039.r: Third Buddhist Council (Pataliputra, Ashoka's reign) → recorded in Sinhalese chronicles Dipavamsa and Mahavamsa; presided by Moggaliputta Tissa.

09-041.r: Mauryan rulers who followed Buddhism → Ashoka and his grandson Dasaratha (who also took the title 'Devanampiya').

09-042.r: Rajjukas → Mauryan rural officials named in Ashoka's edicts; surveyors with judicial and assessment duties.

09-043.r: Pradeshtha (Mauryan) → Justice department, preventing crimes; Arthashastra also mentions a divisional-level Pradeshtha.

09-044.r: Sarthwah (Sarthavaha) → head of a convoy (caravan) of merchants, described in Kautilya's Arthashastra.

09-045.r: Agraharika → not a Mauryan official. Ashoka's 3rd edict names Yukta (revenue), Rajjuka (rural surveyor-judge) and Pradeshika (top divisional official).

09-046.r: Ashokan inscriptions: Pradeshika, Rajuka and Yukta → district-level officers (Pradeshika chief district administrator; Rajuka land measurement, tax, justice; Yukta revenue).
09-046.t: Another book answer calls Pradeshika a divisional head; for IAS 2025 the answer is district-level administration.

09-047.r: Sarnath Pillar → built by Ashoka; four lions back to back = India's national emblem; Mauryan pillars are of Chunar sandstone.

09-048.r: Sanchi Stupa (Raisen district, MP) → considered the best stupa architecturally; built by Ashoka. Bharhut stupa is in Satna district, MP.

09-051.r: Ancient name of Sanchi → Kaknam (Kakanam); a 4th-century CE Gupta inscription calls it 'Kakanam Mahavihara'.
09-051.t: Besnagar (Vidisha) and Dashpura (Mandsaur) are other ancient MP towns, not Sanchi.

09-052.r: Bharhut Stupa (near Satna, MP; built c. 150 BC) → fine example of Shunga architecture.

09-053.r: Sanchi Great Stupa gateway (torana) → shows Ashoka's pilgrimage to the Bodhi tree with his two queens.

09-054.r: Kaushambi → Ghositarama Monastery; Kushinagar → Ranabhar Stupa; Sarnath → Dhamek Stupa; Shravasti → Sahet-Mahet.
09-054.h: Sahet-Mahet sounds like 'Shravasti's twin mounds'; Dhamek = Dhamma first taught at Sarnath.

09-055.r: Ashoka's pilgrimage route → Lumbini, Kapilavastu, Gaya, Sarnath, Kushinagar, Shravasti.
09-055.h: Follows Buddha's life: birth, home, enlightenment, first sermon, death; Shravasti added last.

09-056.r: Ashoka's inscriptions → mostly Prakrit language; three classes: rock, pillar (column) and cave inscriptions; 14 major rock edicts.
09-056.t: Not Pali or Sanskrit; Pali is the language of Buddhist texts.

09-057.r: Ashokan inscriptions → mostly Prakrit language in Brahmi script; Mansehra and Shahbazgarhi → Prakrit in Kharoshthi script. Earliest stone inscriptions were in Prakrit.
09-057.t: Don't confuse language (Prakrit) with script (Brahmi or Kharoshthi).

09-061.r: James Prinsep → first deciphered Brahmi script and first read Ashokan edicts, using letters inscribed on stone tablets.

09-067.r: Ashokan inscriptions near Peshawar (Shahbazgarhi, Mansehra in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa) → Kharosthi script; most others are Brahmi.

09-068.r: Pre-Ashokan Brahmi script → found at Anuradhapura (Sri Lanka); such evidence also from Piparaha, Sohgaura and Mahasthan.

09-069.r: Kharoshthi → ancient script written right to left, of north-west India; deciphered by James Prinsep (1835), Grotefend, Lassen and others.

09-070.r: Kharosthi → cursive script of the Gandhara culture (modern Afghanistan-Pakistan), written right to left.

09-071.r: Ashoka in his inscriptions → 'Priyadarshi' (Piyadasi), 'Devanampiya Piyadasi' (Beloved of the Gods); Puranas call him Ashok Vardhan.

09-074.r: Ashokan pillars → highly polished, monolithic, tapering shaft; NOT parts of architectural structures but independent sculptures.

09-075.r: Kanganahalli stupa (Kalaburagi, Karnataka, on Bhima river) → stone portrait of Ashoka with his queen, labelled 'Ranyo Ashoka'.

09-076.r: Ashoka's personal name appears in the Maski, Gujarra, Nettur and Udagolam edicts; more than 40 Ashokan edicts are known.

09-079.r: Rummindei pillar (Lumbini) → marks Buddha's birthplace; Ashoka exempted Bali tax and cut land revenue from 1/6 to 1/8 there.

09-080.r: Gujarra minor rock edict (names Ashoka) → Datia district, Madhya Pradesh, on the old Ujjain-Bharuch road.

09-081.r: Bhabru (Bairat) inscription → Ashoka calls himself 'Piyadasi Raja Magadha' (king of Magadha); proves he was a Buddhist.

09-082.r: Kalsi (Dehradun district, Uttarakhand) → famous for Ashokan rock edicts.

09-084.r: Ashokan major rock edicts: Dhauli → Odisha; Erragudi → Andhra Pradesh; Jaugada → Odisha (not MP); Kalsi → Uttarakhand (not Karnataka). Two pairs correct.

09-085.r: Rock Edict XII → religious synthesis/tolerance; RE II → South Indian kingdoms and medical care for men and animals; RE XI → policy of Dhamma.

09-086.r: Rock Edict XIII → Kalinga war, victory and Ashoka's remorse; Kalinga conquered eight years after coronation (261 BC).

09-087.r: Kalinga victory → mentioned in Ashoka's Rock Edict XIII, not in Maski, Rudradaman or Hathigumpha inscriptions; so option (e).

09-089.r: Rock Edict XII → wholly devoted to religious tolerance and growth of the essence of all sects.

09-090.r: Ashoka's 12th Major Rock Edict → 'whoever praises his own sect and blames others out of excess devotion injures his own sect' (religious harmony).

09-091.r: Ashoka's edicts → 'All our people should create good deeds… enjoy joy with minds unpolluted with jealousy' (wish for subjects' welfare).
09-091.t: UPPSC's answer key gave Harshavardhana; the book answers Ashoka, saying no source supports the key.

09-092.r: Rock Edicts II and XIII → mention Sangam kingdoms Chola, Pandya, Satiyaputta, Keralaputta and Tamraparni (Sri Lanka); Satavahanas not mentioned.

09-094.r: Rock Edict XIII → Ashoka's five Yavana contemporaries: Antiochus II (Syria), Turamaya = Ptolemy II Philadelphus (Egypt), Antigonus (Macedonia), Mag (Cyrene), Alexander (Epirus).
09-094.h: Turamaya = Ptolemy = Egypt; Antiyoka = Antiochus = Syria.

09-097.r: Ashoka's Dhamma → centred on peace, non-violence and religious toleration (Rock Edict XII); more than one option fits, so (e).
